SARAH.name: Sarah

segs.text: By now Abraham was old and well along in years, and the LORD had blessed him in every way.
So Abraham instructed the chief servant of his household, who managed all he owned,
“Place your hand under my thigh,
and I will have you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I am dwelling,
but will go to my country and my kindred to take a wife for my son Isaac.”
The servant asked him,
“What if the woman is unwilling to follow me to this land? Shall I then take your son back to the land from which you came?”
Abraham replied,
“Make sure that you do not take my son back there.

The LORD, the God of heaven, who brought me from my father’s house and my native land, who spoke to me and promised me on oath, saying, ‘To your offspring I will give this land’—He will send His angel before you so that you can take a wife for my son from there.
And if the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you are released from this oath of mine. Only do not take my son back there.”
So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of his master Abraham and swore an oath to him concerning this matter.
Then the servant took ten of his master’s camels and departed with all manner of good things from his master in hand. And he set out for Nahor’s hometown in Aram-naharaim.
As evening approached, he made the camels kneel down near the well outside the town at the time when the women went out to draw water.
“O LORD, God of my master Abraham,”
he prayed,
“please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham.
Here I am, standing beside the spring, and the daughters of the townspeople are coming out to draw water.

Now may it happen that the girl to whom I say, ‘Please let down your jar that I may drink,’ and who responds, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels as well’—let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac. By this I will know that You have shown kindness to my master.”
Before the servant had finished praying, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham’s brother Nahor.
Now the girl was very beautiful, a virgin who had not had relations with any man. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up again.
So the servant ran to meet her and said,
“Please let me have a little water from your jar.”
“Drink, my lord,”
she replied, and she quickly lowered her jar to her hands and gave him a drink.
After she had given him a drink, she said,
“I will also draw water for your camels, until they have had enough to drink.”
And she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran back to the well to draw water, until she had drawn water for all his camels.
Meanwhile, the man watched her silently to see whether or not the LORD had made his journey a success.
And after the camels had finished drinking, he took out a gold ring weighing a beka, and two gold bracelets for her wrists weighing ten shekels.
“Whose daughter are you?”
he asked.
“Please tell me, is there room in your father’s house for us to spend the night?”
She replied,
“I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son that Milcah bore to Nahor.”
Then she added,
“We have plenty of straw and feed, as well as a place for you to spend the night.”
Then the man bowed down and worshiped the LORD,
saying,

“Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness from my master. As for me, the LORD has led me on the journey to the house of my master’s relatives.”
The girl ran and told her mother’s household about these things.
Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban, and he rushed out to the man at the spring.
As soon as he saw the ring, and the bracelets on his sister’s wrists, and heard Rebekah’s words,
“The man said this to me,”
he went and found the man standing by the camels near the spring.
“Come, you who are blessed by the LORD,”
said Laban.
“Why are you standing out here? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels.”
So the man came to the house, and the camels were unloaded. Straw and feed were brought to the camels, and water to wash his feet and the feet of his companions.
Then a meal was set before the man, but he said,
“I will not eat until I have told you what I came to say.”
So Laban said,
“Please speak.”
“I am Abraham’s servant,”
he replied.
“The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become rich. He has given him sheep and cattle, silver and gold, menservants and maidservants, camels and donkeys.
My master’s wife Sarah has borne him a son in her old age, and my master has given him everything he owns.
My master made me swear an oath and said, ‘You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites in whose land I dwell,
but you shall go to my father’s house and to my kindred to take a wife for my son.’
Then I asked my master, ‘What if the woman will not come back with me?’
And he told me, ‘The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send His angel with you and make your journey a success, so that you may take a wife for my son from my kindred and from my father’s house.
And when you go to my kindred, if they refuse to give her to you, then you will be released from my oath.’
So when I came to the spring today, I prayed: O LORD, God of my master Abraham, if only You would make my journey a success!
Here I am, standing beside this spring. Now if a maiden comes out to draw water and I say to her, ‘Please let me drink a little water from your jar,’
and she replies, ‘Drink, and I will draw water for your camels as well,’ may she be the woman the LORD has appointed for my master’s son.
And before I had finished praying in my heart, there was Rebekah coming out with her jar on her shoulder, and she went down to the spring and drew water. So I said to her, ‘Please give me a drink.’
She quickly lowered her jar from her shoulder and said, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels as well.’ So I drank, and she also watered the camels.
Then I asked her, ‘Whose daughter are you?’ She replied, ‘The daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her wrists.
Then I bowed down and worshiped the LORD; and I blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who led me on the right road to take the granddaughter of my master’s brother for his son.
Now if you will show kindness and faithfulness to my master, tell me; but if not, let me know, so that I may go elsewhere.”
Laban and Bethuel answered,
“This is from the LORD; we have no choice in the matter.
Rebekah is here before you. Take her and go, and let her become the wife of your master’s son, just as the LORD has decreed.”
When Abraham’s servant heard their words, he bowed down to the ground before the LORD.
Then he brought out jewels of silver and gold, and articles of clothing, and he gave them to Rebekah. He also gave precious gifts to her brother and her mother.
Then he and the men with him ate and drank and spent the night there. When they got up the next morning, he said,
“Send me on my way to my master.”
But her brother and mother said,
“Let the girl remain with us ten days or so. After that, she may go.”
But he replied,
“Do not delay me, since the LORD has made my journey a success. Send me on my way so that I may go to my master.”
So they said,
“We will call the girl and ask her opinion.”
They called Rebekah and asked her,
“Will you go with this man?”
“I will go,”
she replied.
So they sent their sister Rebekah on her way, along with her nurse and Abraham’s servant and his men.
And they blessed Rebekah and said to her,
“Our sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands. May your offspring possess the gates of their enemies.”
Then Rebekah and her servant girls got ready, mounted the camels, and followed the man. So the servant took Rebekah and left.
Now Isaac had just returned from Beer-lahai-roi, for he was living in the Negev.
Early in the evening, Isaac went out to the field to meditate, and looking up, he saw the camels approaching.
And when Rebekah looked up and saw Isaac, she got down from her camel
and asked the servant,
“Who is that man in the field coming to meet us?”
“It is my master,”
the servant answered. So she took her veil and covered herself.
Then the servant told Isaac all that he had done.
And Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took Rebekah as his wife. And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death.

card_notes: Every spoken word is Scripture: Genesis 24:1–67, complete.
notes: Text: Genesis 24:1-67 in full, no verses skipped or abridged (1,661 words, the longest unit so far). Speakers: N narrator, A Abraham (same voice as in earlier units), S the servant, R Rebekah, L Laban, LB 'Laban and Bethuel answered' (24:50-51), 'they said' (24:57) and the blessing 'Our sister' (24:60), all given Laban's voice, BM 'her brother and mother said' (24:55) and M 'they ... asked her' (24:58), both given a woman's voice for the mother. Who of a group actually speaks is not in the text: these are defaults that can be changed at assembly by editing 'voices'. The servant speaks the words he quotes from others in 24:37-47, as the text has it. Rebekah's words quoted by the narrator in 24:30 are in her voice. The local BSB snapshot was read verse by verse for this chapter; no slips found.

Still tags: T = from the text, I = inferred, D = dramatized. REF = character reference sheet (not used in the film, no clip). Still 'verses' are chapter:verse; still ids are the verse number plus a letter (07b = second picture of verse 7), clips are V-<still id>.

The servant: the text never names him ('the chief servant of his household, who managed all he owned', 24:2; then 'the servant' and 'the man'). Whether he is Eliezer of Damascus (15:2) is a traditional identification the text does not make, so he is not named anywhere and has a sheet of his own, refs/REF-ABRAHAMS-SERVANT.jpg (key SERVANT): an old man of about seventy with grey hair, in a dark brown tunic and sand-coloured cloak. His skin tone and curly hair do not contradict the ELIEZER block of s02e01c (fifty-five years earlier in the story), and nothing identifies him with it: the picture leaves the question open. His age and looks are I (the Hebrew behind 'chief' is 'elder').

New sheets in this unit: refs/REF-REBEKAH.jpg (key REBEKAH: 'very beautiful', 24:16, is T; her age of about eighteen, her looks and her terracotta-rose dress are I), refs/REF-LABAN.jpg (key LABAN: a man of about twenty-five in a green tunic; I. Genesis 29-31 needs him decades older: derive a new sheet from this one) and refs/REF-ISAAC.jpg (key ISAAC: Isaac at forty, 25:20, bearded, in the cream tunic and red-and-blue cord he has worn since s02e02c; I). Abraham uses refs/REF-ABRAHAM.jpg and Sarah (36a only, a memory of Isaac's birth) refs/REF-SARAH.jpg, descriptions copied word for word from s02e01e. Bethuel, Rebekah's mother, her nurse, her two servant girls and the servant's three men are description blocks without sheets (BETHUEL continues the young Bethuel of s02e02d V1: cream tunic, red cord). The nurse is not named here (35:8 calls her Deborah). The text gives no number for the servant girls (24:61) or for the men with the servant (24:32, 24:54, 24:59): two and three are I.

24:2, 24:9 'hand under my thigh': painted as the text says and no more: the servant kneels beside the seated, fully clothed Abraham with his hand hidden under the thigh between leg and seat (09a). What the gesture meant is not explained.

Where Abraham is living is not stated in this chapter. He is painted in tents under oaks in the hill country of Canaan (I, from 23:2 and 23:19 at Hebron and 24:3 'the Canaanites among whom I am dwelling'), and Isaac in the Negev (T, 24:62). Abraham is not shown after 24:10: the servant calls Isaac 'my master' in 24:65 and reports to Isaac in 24:66, and whether Abraham was still alive or present then is left as the text leaves it (25:7-8 comes later in the narrative).

God is never shown. 'He will send His angel before you' (24:7, 24:40) is painted only as a soft light far ahead on an empty road (07c, 40b: D), never as a figure. 07b (the land under a broad light) pictures the promise quoted in 24:7.

The journey (24:10): the text gives only the start and the destination. The road through the hills and the fording of a great river (10c, 10d) are I, from the name Aram-naharaim ('Aram of the two rivers'). 'Nahor's hometown' (BSB) is painted as an unnamed walled mud-brick town on a northern plain, like the house of s02e02d; whether it is Haran or a town called Nahor is not decided. Camels are shown because the text names them (ten, 24:10); the debate about when camels were first kept in Canaan is not addressed. Ten camels are counted out in 10a and 44b; other pictures show only part of the string. Riders (I): the servant and three men going, and Rebekah, her nurse and the two girls as well on the way back (24:61 'mounted the camels').

The well: the BSB uses both 'well' (24:11, 24:20) and 'spring' (24:13, 24:16, 24:29, 24:30, 24:42-45), and Rebekah 'went down to the spring ... and came up again' (24:16), so it is painted as a spring-fed well: a wide stone-lined pit with steps down to a pool, and a stone trough at ground level (block SPRING; the trough is T, 24:20). The evening hour (24:11) is kept through all the well scenes, darkening to dusk by 24:22-31; the house scenes of 24:32-53 are by lamplight and 24:54 onward in the morning.

The prayer (24:12-14): the servant stands (T, 24:13 'standing beside the spring') and prays without moving his lips (T, 24:45 'praying in my heart'). 24:15 'before the servant had finished praying': Rebekah is seen coming while his eyes are still closed (15b). 15c (Rebekah leaving her father's courtyard) pictures the genealogy of 24:15 and is I. 24:16 'a virgin who had not had relations with any man' is spoken as written and not pictured.

The ring and the bracelets: 24:22 says the servant 'took out' the gold after the camels had drunk and then asked whose daughter she was; 24:47 says he asked first and then 'put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her wrists'. Both are kept: 22b shows him taking the gold out (one ring, two bracelets: T), 23a shows him asking with the gold still closed in his hand, and the putting on is shown after her answer (25b, and again in the retelling, 47a). Rebekah wears no jewellery before 25b and wears the nose ring and both bracelets from 27b on (block JEWELS), as 24:30 requires. The weights (a beka, ten shekels) are spoken as written and not pictured as numbers.

24:26, 24:48, 24:52 'bowed down': kneeling with the forehead to the ground each time; in 24:52 ('to the ground before the LORD') he bows toward an empty wall, away from the family, so that he is not seen bowing to any person.

24:28-31: the pictures follow the text's own order: Rebekah runs to 'her mother's household' (the women of the house: 28b), Laban is introduced (29a), then what he saw and heard (30a, 30b) and his run to the spring (30c). Rebekah leaves her jar at the well when she runs (28a: D). Laban's interest in the gold (29a, 30a, 53c) follows 24:30 'as soon as he saw the ring'; no judgment of his motives is added beyond that.
24:32-33: 'water to wash his feet and the feet of his companions': a boy of the house pours the water (I). The food stays untouched in every picture until 24:54 (T, 24:33).

The servant's account (24:34-49) is pictured partly in the lamplit room (the speaker and his listeners) and partly as what he remembers, painted from new angles so that no picture of 24:1-27 is repeated. 36a: Sarah with the newborn Isaac. 36b: Abraham with his grown son, both seen from behind. 40a: Abraham walking toward a light ('before whom I have walked'). Rebekah listens from a doorway (40c, 47b); the text does not say where she was while he spoke, only that she is 'here before you' in 24:51 (I).

24:50 'Laban and Bethuel answered': both are shown answering (50a), Laban named first as in the text. 24:53 and 24:55 name only 'her brother and her mother', so the gifts go to those two and the request for ten days comes from those two; Bethuel is not shown after 24:51 and the reason for his absence from these verses is not guessed at.

24:60: the blessing is given by the brother and the mother (I: 'they ... our sister'). 'Thousands upon thousands' and 'possess the gates of their enemies' are faceless visions (60b, 60c, the VISION block and the gate picture of s02e02d Q4), with no nation, city or battle identified.

24:62-67: Beer-lahai-roi is not pictured (Isaac has 'just returned' from it); he walks into a small camp in the Negev (62a). 24:63 'to meditate': the BSB word is kept in the narration and he is painted walking alone with bowed head; whether he was praying, mourning or thinking is not decided. 24:64 'got down from her camel' follows the BSB; she is unveiled until 24:65 (T) and veiled from 65c through 67a. 24:67 'the tent of his mother Sarah': a black goat-hair tent like the others (I); 'took Rebekah as his wife' is implied only by the open tent door at dusk (67a) and the two standing hand in hand next morning (67b). 67c (Isaac's hand on a folded indigo shawl, the shawl Sarah wears in every earlier unit) is D.
Style line: 'tents of black goat hair' is left out of the style (lesson of s02e01a); tents are named only in the stills set in the camps.
Narration is not generated in this unit; shots are laid at assembly.
